Barnaby Badger was having a most excellent day. He had just finished digging a new tunnel, a fine, roomy passage leading to a patch of particularly tender earthworms, when his shovel, a sturdy front paw, struck something hard. "What can this be?" Barnaby wondered aloud, pulling it out with a grunt. It was round and flat and shone with a dull, silvery gleam. "A treasure!" he exclaimed, holding it up. "The best treasure I have ever found!"

Just then, Molly Magpie swooped down from a nearby elm. "What have you there, Barnaby?" she asked, her sharp eyes fixed on the shiny object. Molly was known throughout the forest for her love of anything that sparkled.

"It's a treasure, Molly!" Barnaby said proudly. "I found it while digging my new tunnel." He held it out for her to see.

Molly landed on a branch close by, tilting her head. "Oh, Barnaby," she chirped, "that is a moon-stone. A very rare and powerful moon-stone indeed."

Barnaby blinked his small eyes. "A moon-stone? What does it do?"

"Well," Molly began, puffing out her chest, "it brings bad luck if it is kept underground too long. It must be freed from the dark earth, you see, by being given to someone who truly appreciates shiny things. Then it brings good luck to everyone. Otherwise," she added with a dramatic shudder, "who knows what troubles might come?"

Barnaby looked at the shiny stone, then at Molly. He felt a little confused. "But I appreciate shiny things, Molly," he said slowly. "I think it is very pretty."

"Oh, but not in the way a magpie does, Barnaby," Molly insisted. "We magpies have a special connection to moon-stones. It is our duty to protect them and ensure they bring good luck to all." She edged a little closer, her eyes glittering. "Why, if you were to give it to me, I could keep it safe in my nest, where its light would shine for the whole forest."

Barnaby still looked puzzled. He liked the smooth feel of the stone in his paw. "But I found it," he mused. "And I like it right here with me."

A grumbling sound came from behind a nearby clump of ferns. Percy Porcupine slowly emerged, shaking his quills. "Oh, for the love of nuts and berries, Molly Magpie," he said, his voice as scratchy as dry leaves. "Must you always be trying to trick poor Barnaby? That's no moon-stone. That's just an old silver button."

Molly ruffled her feathers, looking rather put out. "It most certainly is not just a button, Percy Porcupine! It is a rare artifact!"

Percy snorted, sending a few quills quivering. "Artifacts do not usually have two small holes in the middle for thread, do they, Barnaby? Let me see that." Barnaby, though still a bit befuddled, held out the object. Percy peered at it. "See? Just as I thought. An old silver button from some farmer's coat, most likely. Lost from a pocket years ago."

Barnaby looked at the object again, turning it over in his paw. Indeed, there were two tiny holes in the center. He had not noticed them before. "A button!" he repeated. "But it is still very shiny and smooth."

Molly Magpie, her plans thwarted, let out an irritated squawk. "Well, if it is just a button, then it is not worth bothering with at all!" she declared, and with a flutter of wings, she flew off towards the distant treetops.

Barnaby watched her go, then looked at his button. "I still like it," he told Percy. "It reminds me of the excellent digging I did to find it."

Percy Porcupine merely grunted. "Good for you, Barnaby. Some folk are just too greedy for their own good. Never mind them." And with that, Percy turned and waddled back into his ferns, secretly pleased that Barnaby had kept his treasure, button or not. Barnaby, quite content, carefully placed his shiny silver button in a special pocket of his new tunnel, pleased that he had found a treasure that was all his own.

Barnaby felt a pang of disappointment. Mr. Crow always had a way of making one feel small. "But it is shiny," he said, trying to defend his treasure.
"Shiny objects are often worthless, Barnaby," Mr. Crow declared, holding the button up for a moment, as if contemplating its true worthlessness. "Indeed, they often attract unwanted attention. Why, I would not be surprised if some thieving creature tried to take such a useless, shiny bauble from you."

"No, Barnaby," Mr. Crow continued, "this button is nothing but trouble. And it is certainly not a sun-stone, nor will it lead you to any treasure. It is just a burden, drawing unwanted eyes to your tunnel. You would be wise to get rid of it."

Or, perhaps, he simply liked the idea of taking something from Barnaby, just because he could.

"Useless, you say, Mr. Crow?" Molly squawked, landing with a flutter just outside the tunnel. "Then why do you still hold it in your claws? If it is truly worthless, you should give it back to Barnaby Chipmunk. After all, he found it fair and square."
Mr. Crow gave Molly Magpie a withering look. "Stay out of this, Molly. This is a matter between Barnaby and me."
"But it is _my_ button, Mr. Crow," Barnaby said, gathering a little courage from Molly Magpie's presence. "Please, may I have it back?"
Mr. Crow sighed dramatically. "Oh, very well, Barnaby," he said, dropping the button carelessly onto the floor of the tunnel. It rolled a short distance before Barnaby quickly scooped it up. "But don't come crying to me when this shiny trifle brings you nothing but trouble."
With that, Mr. Crow flew off, casting a disappointed glance back at the button as he went. He had hoped Barnaby would simply discard it, leaving it for him to pick up later. But Molly Magpie had spoiled his plan.
Molly Magpie, though, did not leave. She turned her bright, beady eyes on Barnaby and the button in his paw. "So, a worthless button, eh?" she said, her voice dripping with skepticism. Barnaby clutched his button tighter. "It is just a button, Molly Magpie. A shiny silver button."
"But it is _very_ shiny," Molly said, her gaze fixed on the object. "And if it is worthless, why did you not throw it away, Barnaby? And why did Mr. Crow not throw it away?"
Barnaby thought for a moment. He truly did not know. He just knew he liked it. "I do not know," he admitted. "But I do not wish to throw it away."
"Well, if you do not want it, Barnaby," Molly began, sidling closer, "I could take it off your paws. I have a collection of shiny things. It would be quite at home with them. And it would save you the trouble of guarding such a 'worthless' item."
Barnaby shook his head. "No, Molly Magpie. It is mine. And I like it right where it is, in my tunnel."
Molly Magpie, seeing that Barnaby was resolute, let out an irritated squawk, much like she had before. "Hmph! Such fuss over a mere button! You are too sentimental, Barnaby Chipmunk. One day, that sentimental heart will get you into trouble."
And with another flutter of wings, Molly Magpie flew off, grumbling to herself about chipmunks and their stubbornness.

Barnaby Chipmunk, left alone once more, looked at his button. It was indeed still shiny. And it was still smooth. And it still made him feel happy. He placed it carefully back into its cranny. He thought of Mr. Crow's words, and Molly Magpie's words, and he even thought of Frisky Squirrel's words. They all seemed to believe his button was worthless, or a source of trouble. But to Barnaby, it was simply beautiful. And he was glad he had found it. He resolved that he would keep it safe, no matter what anyone said. For a treasure, he reasoned, did not have to be gold or jewels to be valuable. Sometimes, a simple, shiny button, found by one's own efforts, could be the greatest treasure of all. And Barnaby Chipmunk was quite content with his treasure. He tucked himself into his bed of dry leaves, still thinking of his shiny button, and soon fell fast asleep.

XIV THE STRANGE SMELL

The days grew shorter and the air grew colder. Winter was certainly on its way, and all the forest-folk were busy. Barnaby Chipmunk had finished filling his storeroom with an impressive collection of beechnuts and acorns. Frisky Squirrel was still scampering about, but even he seemed to be working with a greater sense of urgency. Percy Porcupine was burrowing deeper into his winter den, preparing for his long naps. Mr. Crow, for his part, spent his days perched on the tallest trees, looking south with a wistful expression, considering his options, but still hoping for some stroke of luck that would allow him to stay.

One crisp autumn morning, as Barnaby Chipmunk was enjoying a late breakfast of his favorite wild berries, a most peculiar smell drifted into his tunnel. It was not the scent of pine needles, nor damp earth, nor even the sweet smell of fallen leaves. It was a sharp, acrid smell, like something burning, but not quite like wood smoke. It was a smell that made his nose wrinkle and his eyes water a little.
Barnaby poked his head out of his tunnel entrance. The air outside was clear and bright, and the sun shone pleasantly on the golden and red leaves of the forest. But the strange smell was stronger out here. It seemed to be coming from the direction of Farmer Green's house.
Barnaby had never smelled anything quite like it before. He was a creature of habit and generally preferred things to be predictable. This new smell was most certainly not predictable. It was, in fact, rather unsettling.
He saw Frisky Squirrel scurrying past, a large acorn clutched in his paws. "Frisky!" Barnaby called out. "Do you smell that?"
Frisky Squirrel stopped, sniffing the air. "Smell what, Barnaby?" he asked, then suddenly sneezed a mighty sneeze. "Oh, that! Yes, indeed! A most peculiar odor. It tickles the nose something fierce."
"What do you suppose it is?" Barnaby asked, still wrinkling his nose.
Frisky twitched his whiskers thoughtfully. "I do not know," he said. "It is not a good smell, is it? Not like a fresh nut, or a sweet berry. It reminds me a little of that time Farmer Green tried to burn the old tires from his wagon. But it is not quite the same."
"Do you think it is dangerous?" Barnaby asked, feeling a little prickle of unease down his spine.
"Dangerous?" Frisky repeated, already looking nervous. "Well, I suppose anything strange could be dangerous. Perhaps Farmer Green is up to some new trick! He is always doing something unusual. Remember that time he painted his barn a most peculiar shade of bright yellow?"
Barnaky nodded. He remembered. The yellow barn had been quite an eyesore for a time.
"Well," Frisky continued, "whatever it is, I am too busy to worry about it. My storeroom is not quite full, and winter is almost here. I suggest you do the same, Barnaby. A full belly is the best protection against any strange smells."
And with that, Frisky Squirrel scurried off, leaving Barnaby still sniffing the air, which now seemed to be carrying an even stronger scent of the mysterious odor.

Barnaby Chipmunk tried to ignore the smell. He went back into his tunnel, intending to tidy his collection of dry leaves. But the smell seemed to seep even into his cozy home. It made him feel restless. He simply could not settle. His curiosity, which was usually a rather quiet sort of curiosity, began to prickle at him. He needed to know what this strange smell was.
So, Barnaby, being a creature who liked to solve small mysteries, decided he would investigate. He crept cautiously out of his tunnel, sniffing the air like a tiny detective. The smell was strongest when he headed in the direction of Farmer Green's house, beyond the old stone wall.
He scuttled past Percy Porcupine's den, where he could hear the soft, rumbling snores of the sleeping porcupine. Percy, it seemed, was undisturbed by the strange smell. Barnaby wished he could be so unconcerned.
He reached the edge of the thick undergrowth that bordered Farmer Green's fields. Peeking through the leaves, Barnaby saw nothing out of the ordinary. The fields were empty, the crops long since harvested. The big red barn stood silent, and the yellow farmhouse looked quiet. Yet the smell was unmistakably stronger here. It was quite pungent now, and it made him cough a little.
Barnaby crept closer, keeping low to the ground. He followed his nose, which led him toward the back of the farmhouse, near a small, neglected shed. The smell was emanating from this shed. It was so strong here that Barnaby felt his eyes watering more than ever.
He paused behind a large stack of firewood, trying to make sense of the smell. It was like something old and dusty, mixed with something sharp and chemical. He had heard Farmer Green mention "paint" and "turpentine" sometimes, but he did not know what those things were, only that they often came with peculiar smells.
As he watched, the door of the small shed slowly creaked open. Barnaby held his breath, pressing himself tightly against the woodpile. He expected to see Farmer Green, or perhaps Johnnie Green, but no one appeared. Instead, a small, gray cloud, thick and hazy, drifted out of the shed opening, carrying with it the strange, acrid smell.
Barnaby watched as the cloud dispersed slowly into the clear autumn air. The smell, however, lingered, clinging to the dry leaves and the wood.
He waited for a long time, watching the shed door. But nothing else happened. No one came out, and no new clouds drifted forth.
Barnaby, emboldened by the quiet, crept a little closer to the shed. He wanted to peer inside, just a little, to see what was causing such a powerful and unusual smell. He knew it was risky, for Farmer Green's shed was always filled with tools and strange human contraptions. But his curiosity was too great to be resisted.
He reached the corner of the shed, where a small crack allowed him a glimpse inside. It was dark, and filled with shadows. He could make out vague shapes, old boxes, dusty tools, and cobwebs. But nothing that explained the smell.
Then, Barnaby saw it. On the floor, near the wall, was a small, overturned tin can. A dark, oily liquid had spilled from it, soaking into the wooden floorboards and leaving a dark stain. The strange, pungent smell was strongest right there, coming from the liquid.
Barnaby edged a tiny bit closer, his whiskers twitching, trying to identify the substance. He had never seen anything like it. It was thick and black, and it smelled so strong it made him dizzy. He certainly did not want to touch it.
As he stared at the spilled liquid, Barnaby heard a sudden, loud creak. He looked up, startled. The shed door, which had been slightly ajar, was slowly swinging shut, pushed by a sudden gust of wind.
Barnaby felt a sudden pang of fear. If the door closed completely, he might be trapped inside the shed! He might be trapped with that strange, smelly, black liquid. And he certainly did not want that.
With a squeak of fright, Barnaby turned and darted away from the shed, scrambling back towards the safety of the woodpile. He did not stop until he was well clear of Farmer Green's yard, his heart thumping in his chest like a drum.

He ran all the way back to his tunnel, not stopping until he was safely inside, surrounded by his familiar, comforting store of nuts. He tried to calm his racing heart. The smell, though fainter here, still seemed to follow him.
Barnaby sat for a long moment, catching his breath. He had solved the mystery of the smell, but he felt no satisfaction. Instead, he felt a deeper unease. What was that black liquid? And why did it smell so terrible?
He thought of telling Frisky Squirrel, but Frisky had been too busy. He thought of Percy Porcupine, but Percy was sleeping soundly. He thought of Mr. Crow, but Mr. Crow always made him feel foolish, and besides, Mr. Crow was likely still sulking about the button.
Barnaby decided it was a mystery best kept to himself, for now. It was certainly not a pleasant mystery. And he resolved to stay far away from Farmer Green's shed, and that strange, black, smelly liquid. He would stick to collecting the last few late acorns, and he would appreciate the simple, good smells of the forest, and he would leave the strange smells and the even stranger liquids to Farmer Green. He curled up in his bed of leaves, trying to forget the acrid odor, and hoped the next day would bring only familiar, comforting smells.

Frisky Squirrel stopped, sniffing the air. "Smell what, Barnaby?" he asked, then suddenly sneezed a mighty sneeze. "Oh, that! Yes, indeed! A most peculiar odor. It tickles the nose something fierce."
"What do you suppose it is?" Barnaby asked, still wrinkling his nose.
Frisky twitched his whiskers thoughtfully. "I do not know," he said. "It is not a good smell, is it? Not like a fresh nut, or a sweet berry. It reminds me a little of that time Farmer Green tried to burn the old tires from his wagon. But it is not quite the same."
"Do you think it is dangerous?" Barnaby asked, feeling a little prickle of unease down his spine.
"Dangerous?" Frisky repeated, already looking nervous. "Well, I suppose anything strange could be dangerous. Perhaps Farmer Green is up to some new trick! He is always doing something unusual. Remember that time he painted his barn a most peculiar shade of bright yellow?"
Barnaky nodded. He remembered. The yellow barn had been quite an eyesore for a time.
"Well," Frisky continued, "whatever it is, I am too busy to worry about it. My storeroom is not quite full, and winter is almost here. I suggest you do the same, Barnaby. A full belly is the best protection against any strange smells."
And with that, Frisky Squirrel scurried off, leaving Barnaby still sniffing the air, which now seemed to be carrying an even stronger scent of the mysterious odor.

Barnaby Chipmunk tried to ignore the smell. He went back into his tunnel, intending to tidy his collection of dry leaves. But the smell seemed to seep even into his cozy home. It was quite pungent now, and it made him cough a little.

He paused behind a large stack of firewood, trying to make sense of the smell. It was like something old and dusty, mixed with something sharp and chemical. He had heard Farmer Green mention "paint" and "turpentine" sometimes, but he did not know what those things were, only that they often came with peculiar smells.
As he watched, the door of the small shed slowly creaked open. Barnaby held his breath, pressing himself tightly against the woodpile. He expected to see Farmer Green, or perhaps Johnnie Green, but no one appeared. Instead, a small, gray cloud, thick and hazy, drifted out of the shed opening, carrying with it the strange, acrid smell.
Barnaby watched as the cloud dispersed slowly into the clear autumn air. The smell, however, lingered, clinging to the dry leaves and the wood.
He waited for a long time, watching the shed door. But nothing else happened. No one came out, and no new clouds drifted forth.
Barnaby, emboldened by the quiet, crept a little closer to the shed. He wanted to peer inside, just a little, to see what was causing such a powerful and unusual smell. He knew it was risky, for Farmer Green's shed was always filled with tools and strange human contraptions. But his curiosity was too great to be resisted.
He reached the corner of the shed, where a small crack allowed him a glimpse inside. It was dark, and filled with shadows. He could make out vague shapes, old boxes, dusty tools, and cobwebs. But nothing that explained the smell.
Then, Barnaby saw it. On the floor, near the wall, was a small, overturned tin can. A dark, oily liquid had spilled from it, soaking into the wooden floorboards and leaving a dark stain. The strange, pungent smell was strongest right there, coming from the liquid.
Barnaby edged a tiny bit closer, his whiskers twitching, trying to identify the substance. He had never seen anything like it. It was thick and black, and it smelled so strong it made him dizzy. He certainly did not want to touch it.
As he stared at the spilled liquid, Barnaby heard a sudden, loud creak. He looked up, startled. The shed door, which had been slightly ajar, was slowly swinging shut, pushed by a sudden gust of wind.
Barnaby felt a sudden pang of fear. If the door closed completely, he might be trapped inside the shed! He might be trapped with that strange, smelly, black liquid. And he certainly did not want that.
With a squeak of fright, Barnaby turned and darted away from the shed, scrambling back towards the safety of the woodpile. He did not stop until he was well clear of Farmer Green's yard, his heart thumping in his chest like a drum.

He ran all the way back to his tunnel, not stopping until he was safely inside, surrounded by his familiar, comforting store of nuts. He tried to calm his racing heart. The smell, though fainter here, still seemed to follow him.
Barnaby sat for a long moment, catching his breath. He had solved the mystery of the smell, but he felt no satisfaction. Instead, he felt a deeper unease. What was that black liquid? And why did it smell so terrible?
He thought of telling Frisky Squirrel, but Frisky had been too busy. He thought of Percy Porcupine, but Percy was sleeping soundly. He thought of Mr. Crow, but Mr. Crow always made him feel foolish, and besides, Mr. Crow was likely still sulking about the button.
Barnaby decided it was a mystery best kept to himself, for now. It was certainly not a pleasant mystery. And he resolved to stay far away from Farmer Green's shed, and that strange, black, smelly liquid. He would stick to collecting the last few late acorns, and he would appreciate the simple, good smells of the forest, and he would leave the strange smells and the even stranger liquids to Farmer Green. He curled up in his bed of leaves, trying to forget the acrid odor, and hoped the next day would bring only familiar, comforting smells.

"What in the world is that?" Sandy asked, his eyes wide. He took a cautious step closer, then another. The strange, slightly chemical smell was much stronger here.

"It looks like one of those cans Farmer Green uses for his engine oil," Frisky said, sniffing carefully. "But it's not engine oil. Engine oil smells like... like engine oil. This smells different. "Maybe it's one of Farmer Green's experiments," Sandy suggested. "You know how he is always trying out new things. Remember that time he tried to make glow-in-the-dark paint for his barn, and it ended up just making the barn smell like old eggs?"

"Whatever it is," Frisky said, "it doesn't look like it belongs here. And it certainly smells like it could be causing trouble for the minnows and the frogs." He looked around. "Where's Mr. Crow now? He was supposed to be supervising."

"Aha!" Mr. Crow proclaimed, puffing out his chest. "I knew my brilliant strategy would yield results! I observed your careful approach, your diligent scrutiny of the environment, and I guided you, with my superior aerial surveillance, to this very spot! And what, pray tell, have you discovered, my keen-nosed lieutenants?"

Sandy Chipmunk looked up at Mr. Crow. "We found this, Mr. Crow," he said, pointing to the seeping can. "It's making a strange smell, and this reddish liquid is dripping out of it, down to the stream."

Mr. Crow peered down at the can, his head cocked to one side. "Indeed!" he declared. "An excellent discovery! Precisely the sort of anomaly one expects to find when a 'foul-smelling mystery' is afoot! It is clearly a discarded container, undoubtedly from Farmer Green's latest ill-conceived venture into modern agriculture."

"But what is it, Mr. Crow?" Frisky Squirrel asked. "And what should we do about it? It looks like it's been leaking for a while."

Mr. Crow hopped along the branch, peering with exaggerated seriousness at the can. "Its precise chemical composition, my dear Squirrel, is a matter for a more thorough, laboratory-based analysis, which, regrettably, we are not equipped to conduct in the field. However, its properties as a pollutant are self-evident! This viscous liquid, with its peculiar shimmering, is undoubtedly the cause of the minnows' dizziness, the water-skaters' confusion, and the frogs' uncharacteristic reticence! It is a poison, my friends, a silent killer of the stream!"

"A poison!" Sandy exclaimed, taking a hurried step back from the can. "Then we must do something! We can't just let it keep dripping into the water!"

"Precisely my thought, Sandy!" Mr. Crow declared, preening. "But what, indeed, is to be done? One cannot simply touch a 'silent killer' with impunity. It requires a delicate touch, a careful approach, and a strategic plan of removal." He looked down at the chipmunk and the squirrel. "You, my agile friends, are perfectly suited for such a task. Your small size and nimble paws would allow you to approach the object without undue risk, and perhaps, with a clever maneuver, to dislodge it from its current position and roll it far from the stream!"

As for the danger, a quick roll, a push with a stick, surely that is not beyond your considerable capabilities. I, of course, shall continue my aerial surveillance, providing guidance and strategic advice from above, ensuring your safety and the success of the mission!"

"Mr. Crow," he began, "if it is truly a poison, then perhaps we should not be the ones to touch it at all. Perhaps Barnaby Beaver, with his strong tail, could perhaps move it, or cover it with mud? The strange smell was still present, but it was no longer dripping into the soil that led to the stream.

He gestured grandly with a wing towards the relocated can.

"Why, that's one of Farmer Green's old cans for his new 'rust-proofing' liquid for his tractor!" he exclaimed. "He was complaining only last week that he couldn't find the last one. "Well, Mr. Crow," he said, turning back to the crow, "whatever you call it, the minnows will thank you, and the frogs will sing your praises. You certainly stirred everyone into action, and that was needed."

Mr. Crow fluffed his feathers, a satisfied gleam in his eye. "Indeed, Barnaby! A leader, my dear fellow, is one who recognizes a problem, formulates a plan, and inspires others to execute it! And that, I flatter myself, is precisely what I have done today! Another crisis averted, another triumph for reason and sagacity in Pleasant Valley!" He then turned to Sandy and Frisky. "You two, of course, have earned a respite. Sandy Chipmunk and Frisky Squirrel merely nodded, already planning to find a quiet place for a well-deserved nap. They knew Mr. Crow's "full, detailed report" would mostly be about Mr. Crow, but they also knew that without his dramatic prodding, the rusty can might still be dripping into the stream, and the minnows might still be swimming in circles. Sometimes, even a self-important crow could do a great deal of good, simply by making a fuss. And sometimes, it seemed, a little bit of exaggeration was just what was needed to get things done in Pleasant Valley.
They watched as Mr. Crow, with another triumphant caw, launched himself into the air, already practicing phrases for his grand speech. He soared towards the Old Mill Pond, no doubt to relay his version of events to the frogs and mussels, and to inform them, with much flourish, that their silence and scarcity were soon to be things of the past. Sandy and Frisky knew that the truth would get somewhat muddled in the retelling, as stories always did when Mr. Crow was the primary narrator. But for now, the sun shone brightly, the strange chemical smell was fading, and the stream flowed on, already beginning to clear. And that, they agreed, was quite enough for one day's work.

Sandy, stretching out his tired paws, remembered the time Mr. Crow had asked him to gather food, leading to the great corn-or-beechnuts debate. Mr. Crow was always asking for help, always with some grand scheme or another, and always taking the credit. But in this case, the help had actually been helpful, and the credit, however disproportionately claimed, was for a good deed done. Perhaps, Sandy thought, Mr. Crow was not quite so bad after all, even if he did talk too much. Or perhaps, Sandy mused further, it was simply that a crisis, even a small, smelly one, brought out the best, or at least the most energetic, in everyone, even Mr. Crow.

Frisky, meanwhile, had already scampered off to inspect a patch of wild berries. "Come on, Sandy!" he called. "All this detective work has made me hungry! And after all that talk about 'alimentary canals,' a good meal sounds like a most agreeable prospect!" Sandy grinned and followed, leaving the scene of their small triumph to the benevolent, if somewhat pompous, oversight of Mr. Crow, who was now delivering a passionate, if highly embellished, account of the day's events to a sleepy turtle on a sun-warmed log by the Old Mill Pond. The turtle, being a creature of profound patience, merely blinked slowly, perhaps already accustomed to the grand pronouncements of Mr. Crow.

The river, however, seemed to breathe a sigh of relief. Slowly but surely, the faint, shimmering film began to dissipate, carried away by the gentle current. The minnows, though still a little wobbly, started to swim with a clearer purpose, their tiny tails flicking with renewed vigor. And in the shallower, sunnier spots, a water-skater, no longer bumping blindly, darted across the surface with its accustomed grace, as if testing the waters of a new, cleaner day. Even the frogs, deep within their reedy hiding places, began to stir, a low, hesitant croak breaking the long silence, a quiet prelude to the boisterous chorus they would surely resume by nightfall, grateful for the efforts of their forest neighbors, and perhaps, even for the unwitting guidance of a certain self-important crow.

The sun began its slow descent, casting long, golden shadows across Pleasant Valley. The air grew cooler, and the faint, unpleasant odor near the oak tree grew fainter still. Farmer Green, coming out to fetch his newspaper from the mailbox at the crossroads, paused, scratching his head. He noticed a peculiar, discarded metal can somewhat out of place in the underbrush, smelling faintly of something familiar, but he merely shrugged. "Always forgetting where I put things," he muttered to himself, and with a casual kick, he rolled the can further into the denser woods, where it would bother no one, and where it would eventually, in time, rust away to nothing. He knew nothing of the crisis averted, or of the bustling efforts of his small forest neighbors. He merely went about his business, as humans often do, oblivious to the dramas and triumphs unfolding all around them in the quiet, green heart of Pleasant Valley.

Meanwhile, back by the stream, a lone water-skater, bolder than the rest, performed a quick, intricate dance across the water's surface, its tiny legs making perfect dimples. It was a silent testament to the return of order, a small, yet significant, sign that the river, which had for a brief time held its breath, was now flowing freely once more. And for the forest folk, that was the most important news of all, far more significant than any of Mr. Crow's grand pronouncements, or Farmer Green's forgotten cans. For the health of the stream was the health of Pleasant Valley, and the return of its natural rhythm was cause for a quiet, contented sigh of relief from every creature, great and small, who called that peaceful valley home.
